# Animated navigation route display (2026-02-06 17:12Z)

_**User**_

I have added the https://github.com/bietiekay/AnimatedPolylineKit  AnimatedPolylineKit to the app dependencies.

Now I want to integrate it to be used when displaying routes between two devices in navigate mode.

It should play a default animation (like the one in the @Libraries/AnimatedPolylineKit-main/Sample/AnimatedMapPolyline/ContentView.swift of the demo app. It should only animate the initial portion of the navigation route in the correct direction of routing.

---

_**Agent (model default, mode Agent)**_

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>

The user wants to integrate AnimatedPolylineKit into their miataru iOS app for displaying routes between two devices in "navigate mode". Key requirements:

1. Use AnimatedPolylineKit (already added as dependency)
2. Display animated polyline when showing routes between two devices in navigate mode
3. Default animation similar to the demo app's ContentView.swift
4. Only animate the **initial portion** of the navigation route (not the full route)
5. Animate in the **correct direction** of routing

I need to:
1. Understand how routes are currently displayed in the app (navigate mode, device-to-device)
2. Look at the demo ContentView.swift to understand the default animation setup
3. Understand how to show only the "initial portion" of the route - this could mean:
   - Only a segment near the start (e.g. first 10% of the route)
   - Or animate progress along the route but only for a portion
   - Or show a short animated segment that moves along the route
4. Ensure direction matches routing direction (start→end or end→start)

Let me search the codebase for:
- Where navigate mode is implemented
- Where routes between devices are drawn (MKPolyline, overlays, etc.)
- How the route coordinates/polyline are obtained

I'll also read the demo ContentView to see the default config and usage pattern.
</details></think>

        "contents": "    private func updateNavigationOverlayStep() {\n        guard let route,\n              let navigationOverlayViewModel,\n              let location = locationManager.currentLocation else { return }\n        guard var stepIndex = closestStepIndex(for: route, to: location.coordinate) else { return }\n        // Never show \"Arrive at destination\" unless user is actually near the destination\n        let lastIndex = route.steps.count - 1\n        if stepIndex == lastIndex, lastIndex &gt; 0 {\n            let lastStep = route.steps[lastIndex]\n            let userPoint = MKMapPoint(location.coordinate)\n            let distanceToDestination = lastStep.polyline.closestDistance(to: userPoint) ?? The navigation view uses SwiftUI's `Map(position:...)` exclusively — no MKMapView. AnimatedPolylineKit uses `MKOverlay` and `MKOverlayRenderer`, which only work with `MKMapView`. SwiftUI's Map doesn't support custom overlay renderers.

SwiftUI Map doesn't support custom MKOverlayRenderer. We could:
- Keep the existing Map and MapPolyline for the route.
- Add an **additional** layer: a transparent UIViewRepresentable that wraps an MKMapView, perfectly overlaid on the Map, only for drawing the AnimatedPolylineOverlay. We'd need to keep camera/region in sync between the two. This is fragile (two maps, sync issues).

              "file": "./Libraries/AnimatedPolylineKit-main/CHANGES.md",
              "matches": [
                {
                  "lineNumber": 1,
                  "content": "# AnimatedPolylineKit – Changes and Decisions"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 12,
                  "content": "- **Public API**: New types in &#96;Sources/AnimatedPolylineKit/&#96;:"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 13,
                  "content": "  - **AnimatedPolylineConfiguration** – Colors, patch size, direction, duration, easing, line style."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 14,
                  "content": "  - **AnimatedPolylineOverlay** – Custom &#96;MKOverlay&#96; holding route coordinates, config, and progress (0…1)."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 15,
                  "content": "  - **AnimatedPolylineRenderer** – Draws full route + moving patch with gradient."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 16,
                  "content": "  - **AnimatedPolylineAnimationDriver** – Drives progress with &#96;CADisplayLink&#96;, optional looping, easing."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 17,
                  "content": "  - **AnimatedPolylineEasingHelper** – Eased progress for manual animation."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 34,
                  "content": "- **AnimatedPolylineOverlay**: Conforms to &#96;MKOverlay&#96; only (no &#96;@MainActor&#96;) so MapKit can use it from any thread without “crosses into main actor” warnings."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 37,
                  "content": "  - **AnimatedPolylineOverlayRegistry** maps &#96;ObjectIdentifier(overlay)&#96; → weak renderer."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 60,
                  "content": "- **AnimatedPolylineAnimationDriver**: Uses &#96;CADisplayLink&#96; on the main run loop; publishes &#96;progress&#96; in [0,1] with configurable duration and start/end easing (blended over the run)."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 69,
                  "content": "  - Builds **AnimatedPolylineOverlay** from &#96;MKPolyline&#96; when a route is received."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 70,
                  "content": "  - Uses **AnimatedPolylineAnimationDriver** and subscribes to &#96;$progress&#96; to set &#96;overlay.progress&#96; on the main thread."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 72,
                  "content": "- **MapView**: Takes &#96;animatedOverlay: AnimatedPolylineOverlay?&#96;; in &#96;rendererFor overlay&#96; returns **AnimatedPolylineRenderer** for that overlay type."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 73,
                  "content": "- **Package reference**: Local package path set to &#96;..&#96; (parent of &#96;Sample/&#96;) so the package at repo root is used; app target links product **AnimatedPolylineKit**."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 87,
                  "content": "- **Sources/AnimatedPolylineKit/**  "
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 88,
                  "content": "  &#96;AnimatedPolylineKit.swift&#96;, &#96;AnimatedPolylineConfiguration.swift&#96;, &#96;AnimatedPolylineOverlay.swift&#96;, &#96;AnimatedPolylineRenderer.swift&#96;, &#96;AnimationDriver.swift&#96;"
                }
              ]
            },

                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 21,
                  "content": "- **Fully configurable from your app**: colors, patch length, highlight strength, animation duration, easing, line width, cap, and join. The package does not hardcode any of these; you supply a complete &#96;AnimatedPolylineConfiguration&#96;."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 25,
                  "content": "- &#96;AnimatedPolylineConfiguration&#96; – all visual and animation settings (colors, gradients, speed, easing, line style)."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 26,
                  "content": "- &#96;AnimatedPolylineOverlay&#96; – the MapKit overlay that holds coordinates and configuration."

                {
                  "lineNumber": 27,
                  "content": "- &#96;AnimatedPolylineRenderer&#96; – draws the polyline and the moving patch on the map."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 28,
                  "content": "- &#96;AnimatedPolylineAnimationDriver&#96; – drives progress from 0 to 1 with optional looping (uses your config for duration and easing)."
                },

                  "lineNumber": 34,
                  "content": "### AnimatedPolylineConfiguration"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 42,
                  "content": "The same configuration is used by both the **overlay** (for drawing) and the **animation driver** (for duration and easing).                 },

                  "content": "### AnimatedPolylineOverlay"

                  "lineNumber": 51,

                  "lineNumber": 58,

                  "lineNumber": 74,

                  "lineNumber": 94,
                  "content": "### AnimatedPolylineEasingHelper"
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 96,
                  "content": "A small **static helper** that applies the same blended start/end easing to a raw time value &#96;t&#96; in [0, 1]. Use it when you drive progress yourself (e.g. with a &#96;Timer&#96; or SwiftUI animation) instead of using &#96;AnimatedPolylineAnimationDriver&#96;."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 106,
                  "content": "- Creates an &#96;AnimatedPolylineOverlay&#96; with a custom &#96;AnimatedPolylineConfiguration&#96; (blue line, 2.5 s cycle, easeIn/easeOut, etc.)."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 107,
                  "content": "- Uses &#96;AnimatedPolylineAnimationDriver&#96; to drive the overlay’s progress and show the moving highlight."
                },
                {
                  "lineNumber": 127,
                  "content": "2. Enter the repository URL (e.g. &#96;https://github.com/bietiekay/AnimatedPolylineKit&#96;)."

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>

We have:
- `route.distance` (CLLocationDistance) from MKRoute
- `route.polyline.split(at: distance)` to get the first segment
- RouteStyle.remaining (blue) for the main route color — we can use that for the animated segment to match
- Direction: when `isRouteReversed` is true, the route is drawn device→user, so the "direction of routing" is from device to user (start = device, end = user). When false, route is user→device. The polyline from MKDirections is always in source→destination order. So when isRouteReversed: request.source = device, request.destination = user → polyline is device→user. When not reversed: source = user, destination = device → polyline is user→device. So "correct direction of routing" means the patch should move in the direction of travel: startToEnd (first coordinate toward last). So we always use .startToEnd for the overlay because the initial-portion polyline we build is already from route start to route end (first 15%); the kit's startToEnd moves the patch from start toward end, which matches "direction of routing". We don't need to flip to endToStart when isRouteReversed — the polyline itself is already in the correct order (from request source to destination). So direction is always .startToEnd for the initial segment. Good.

Now for the overlay approach. We need a UIViewRepresentable that:
1. Is non-interactive (userInteractionEnabled = false) so touches pass through to the SwiftUI Map
2. Takes: region (MKCoordinateRegion), initialPortionPolyline (MKPolyline?), direction (we said startToEnd always)
3. Has an MKMapView that only shows the animated overlay (no base map? No — we need the overlay to draw on something. Actually the overlay is drawn ON the map. So the MKMapView would need to show the same map content as the SwiftUI Map, or we make it fully transparent and only draw the overlay. If the MKMapView is transparent, we'd see the SwiftUI Map through it, and the overlay would be drawn on top. But MKMapView has a map background — we need the map view to be transparent so the SwiftUI Map shows through. MapKit's MKMapView can have a transparent background? Let me check — typically the map view draws the map tiles. So if we put an MKMapView on top with the same region, it would show its own map tiles and we'd have two maps. To get "only the overlay" we need either (1) a transparent MKMapView that doesn't draw the map (not really supported — we could set the map type to something and make the view clear, but the map still draws), or (2) a view that isn't an MKMapView but that can draw the overlay. Option 2 isn't possible because the overlay renderer is called by MapKit when the overlay is added to an MKMapView. So we must use an MKMapView. The only way to have "only the overlay" visible is to have the MKMapView with a transparent/clear background. In iOS, MKMapView doesn't support a fully transparent map that shows another view through it for the base map — the map view will draw its own tiles. So the hybrid approach (Map + transparent MKMapView with only overlay) would result in the overlay being drawn on the MKMapView's map, and we'd see two maps stacked (the MKMapView would obscure the SwiftUI Map unless the MKMapView's frame is zero or we use a custom container). Actually: we could make the MKMapView's frame cover the map and set the map's alpha to 0 (or use a clear map type if it exists). Then we'd see through to the SwiftUI Map... But MKMapView doesn't have a "clear" map type. So we'd have to use a different approach: put the MKMapView behind the SwiftUI Map (in ZStack order: MKMapView first, then Map). Then the Map is on top and the user interacts with it. The MKMapView below would need to show the same region and the same route (so the user sees one map). But then the animated overlay on the MKMapView would be behind the SwiftUI Map and not visible. So that doesn't work.

The only way to have a single map and an animated overlay is to have the map be an MKMapView so we can add the overlay. So we need to replace the SwiftUI Map with an MKMapView-based representable when in navigate mode (or always in this view). That's the full refactor: implement a NavigationMapView (UIViewRepresentable) that:
- Takes mapPosition (or region), annotations (user + device markers), route (full route polyline + optional initial-portion for animation), isRouteReversed, isMutualNavigation, showRouteProgress, etc.
- Uses MKMapView, sets region from mapPosition, adds annotations, adds MKPolyline for the full route (with standard renderer), adds AnimatedPolylineOverlay for the initial portion with AnimatedPolylineRenderer
- Handles map style, compass, scale bar could stay as overlays

I have enough to write the plan. The key constraint is that AnimatedPolylineKit requires MKMapView (MKOverlay/MKOverlayRenderer). So we have two viable approaches:

**Approach A – Full MKMapView replacement**
Replace `baseMapView` (the SwiftUI `Map`) with a custom `UIViewRepresentable` that wraps `MKMapView`, replicates all current map content (annotations, route polylines with done/todo/ghost logic), and adds the animated overlay for the initial portion. Requires:
- New representable that takes region/camera binding (or MapCameraPosition), annotations, route, showRouteProgress, isRouteReversed, isMutualNavigation, etc.
- Delegate to sync map position back (regionDidChange) and to provide overlay renderers (standard MKPolylineRenderer for route segments, AnimatedPolylineRenderer for the animated overlay).
- Converting MapCameraPosition ↔ MKMapView region/camera so the rest of the view (reset zoom, follow mode, etc.) keeps working.

**Approach B – Overlay-only MKMapView on top (two-map approach)**
Keep the SwiftUI Map. Add a second, non-interactive view on top that draws only the animated segment. The problem: that view must be an MKMapView to use AnimatedPolylineRenderer, and an MKMapView always draws the base map. So we'd see two base maps. Workaround: make the top MKMapView's background clear and use a map type that looks "empty" — but MapKit doesn't offer that. So we'd have to make the overlay map view's frame match and set its map to the same style; then we'd have two identical maps stacked, and the top one would only add the overlay. When the user pans, we'd pan the SwiftUI Map; we'd need to sync the overlay map's region in updateUIView from currentRegion. The overlay map would have isUserInteractionEnabled = false so touches pass through to the Map. But "pass through" might not work as expected — the overlay view might still capture touches. We could set isUserInteractionEnabled = false on the overlay MKMapView so that touches go to the view behind it (the Map). So the user interacts with the Map; the Map's onMapCameraChange updates currentRegion; in the overlay representable's updateUIView we set the overlay map's region to currentRegion. So both maps stay in sync. The overlay map would show the same map type and same region, and on top of that we add only the AnimatedPolylineOverlay. So we'd see one map (the SwiftUI Map) and one overlay (the animated segment). Wait — if the overlay view is on top with the same frame, we'd see the overlay map's content (map tiles + overlay). So we'd see the overlay map, not the SwiftUI Map. So the "top" view would be what the user sees. If we make the overlay map non-interactive, touches would pass through to the Map below. So the user would be panning the Map below, but seeing the overlay map on top. The two would go out of sync until the next updateUIView (when currentRegion updates). So we need to update the overlay map's region on every camera change. That's doable. So the flow: Map (bottom) receives gestures, updates mapPosition and currentRegion. Overlay view (top) has same frame, isUserInteractionEnabled = false, and in updateUIView we set overlay MKMapView.region = currentRegion. So the overlay map's region is always synced. We'd see the overlay map (same tiles as the one below) plus the animated overlay. So we have two maps drawing the same thing, and the top one also draws the animated segment. This is redundant (two map tile renders) but would work. Let me add this as "Approach B" in the plan and recommend Approach A for a single map and cleaner architecture, but mention B as a less invasive option with the caveat of two map layers.
